This paper proposes the WenMind benchmark, which is designed to evaluate LLMs in Chinese Classical Literature and Language Arts (CCLLA) across Ancient Prose, Ancient Poetry, and Ancient Literary Culture. WenMind includes 4,875 question-answer pairs, 42 fine-grained tasks, three question formats, and two evaluation scenarios. A comprehensive evaluation of 31 LLMs, including general-purpose and ancient Chinese models, reveals that the top-performing model, ERNIE-4.0, achieves only 64.3%, highlighting the need for improvement. 

Strengths:
1. This paper is well-organized and easy to read.
2. This paper investigates the efficacy of LLMs in the CCLLA domain, contributing to an underexplored area in the field.
3. The development of the WenMind benchmark represents a significant advancement in fostering transparency and invites further research and development within the CCLLA community.
4. The experimental results are comprehensive, highlighting the need for improvement of LLMs for CCLLA. 

Weaknesses:
1. More details about the data collection and data annotations should be included.
2. The evaluation should be improved by providing more automatic metrics and using more powerful LLMs for evaluating the quality of the models.

Thank you very much for your valuable feedback. We agree with your important points regarding the use of simplified and traditional Chinese characters in evaluating LLMs’ ability to understand classical Chinese texts. 

To address this, we propose the following improvements:   
(1) We will provide datasets in both simplified and traditional characters as soon as possible.  
(2) We conduct separate evaluations using both character sets and perform comparative analysis of results from simplified and traditional character datasets.  

Due to space and time constraints, we only provide experimental results for three models here. The complete experimental results and analysis will be added to the supplementary materials in the final version.

|:-------:|:-------:|
|Qwen1.5-14B-Chat|42.8|
|Baichuan2-7B-Chat|30.1|
|Bloom-7B-Chunhua|25.8|

Thank you for your time and effort on author response. Your additional response on Q2-Q6 resolved my remaining concerns.

However, I don't agree with your response to Q1. As the major difference between Classical Chinese and modern Chinese lies in the difference in their characters, your benchmarks and evaluation results, which were written and tested on simplified Chinese for modern Chinese, may not fully examine the capabilities of LLMs in understanding Classical Chinese. Instead of adding a section with Classical Chinese data written in traditional Chinese characters, I believe you should replace all your data written in simplified Chinese with the original form, which would be traditional Chinese.

I would like to keep my score.

Thank you for your careful review of our paper and the valuable comments. We have taken your concerns about ethical issues seriously and are responding to each one individually.

> Q1: Potential issues with data collection.

A1: We are indeed aware that the automated collection of data or generation through LLMs may introduce noise or harmful information. To mitigate this risk, we have conducted rigorous cleaning and screening after data collection and generation. 

(1) Data Collection Process

Table 2 in the supplementary materials categorizes the data collection methods into five types. Here is a detailed explanation:

① Data collected from the internet. Collectors: Volunteer A, Volunteer B, and Graduate Student C. Collection process: Based on common tasks in Chinese language exams (reading comprehension, understanding-based recitation, etc.), collect high-quality exam questions made by experts and scholars from the internet. We require that the questions should be closely matched with the tasks.

② Other open-source datasets. Collector: Graduate Student D. Collection process: The data collector conducts research and collection of existing open-source datasets, selects classic tasks and high-quality data in the CCLLA field, and assesses the scarcity and construction difficulty of task data. Ultimately, valuable and currently scarce data are selected for reuse to supplement and improve the evaluation benchmark. 
Post-processing: a. Text filtering: Perform operations such as handling of abnormal symbols (e.g., blank squares), deletion of irrelevant content (e.g., "\r"), and after manual inspection, obtain complete and high-quality data. b. Question writing: Construct Q&A pairs oriented by the needs of different tasks. c. Standardization of format: Questions for the same task are unified into the same questioning method. We directly set up corresponding question templates according to different tasks.

③ LLMs. Collector: Graduate Student E. The construction process refers to lines 123-126 of the main text.

(2) Data Review Process

① Reviewers: The review is conducted by three individuals, namely Volunteer A, Graduate Student D, and Graduate Student E.
② A total of approximately 7000 data entries were collected. The reviewers manually verified the Q&A pairs from three dimensions: the standardization and accuracy of the questions, the correctness and comprehensiveness of the answers, and whether the text content contains ethical issues or unsafe content.
③ Data with non-standard Q&A were deleted or revised, and entries with safety issues were excluded.
④ Finally, the remaining data were rebalanced in terms of task and quality, followed by a second round of proofreading.


> Q2: The Ancient Prose dataset is "ancient", so it likely reinforces some social stereotypes.

A2: We fully recognize that there may be ethical issues such as social stereotypes in ancient texts. After data review, there may still be some omissions. We believe that the content of ancient texts is of great significance for academic research and education, as these contents reflect the social reality of history. In our paper, we will clearly emphasize the historical and academic value of these contents, which does not mean that we agree with or spread these stereotypes. Our dataset is mainly used for research on historical texts, language transformation, ancient scenes, etc., and does not encourage or allow it to be used to reinforce or spread social prejudices.

> Q3: The authors should consider potential downstream applications of these text generations. 

A3: For the task of generating ancient texts, poetry, or other literary forms, we believe it holds significant academic and educational value. For instance, it can be used to study the linguistic structure of ancient texts, cultural dissemination, and the techniques of poetry creation. It can also enhance students' understanding of ancient literature in language education settings. We will further emphasize the academic uses of these text generations in our paper and suggest that users only utilize these generated contents within academic and educational contexts. Moreover, we are aware of the potential risks of misuse, and therefore, we will clearly define the scope of use in our paper to prevent the generated content from being used for improper purposes.

>Q4: Acknowledgment and discussion of ethical issues.

A4: In the original paper, we did not fully discuss the ethical issues, which was an oversight on our part. We will include a dedicated section in the final version to discuss the ethical considerations of the dataset in detail. We will acknowledge the potential social, cultural, and historical risks that may exist in the dataset and discuss how to mitigate these risks when using it. At the same time, we will clarify the scope of the dataset, emphasizing its academic and historical significance, to prevent its misuse.

③ LLMs. Collector: Graduate Student E. The construction process refers to lines 123-126 of the main text.

① Reviewers: The review is conducted by three individuals, namely Volunteer A, Graduate Student D, and Graduate Student E.
② A total of approximately 7000 data entries were collected. The reviewers manually verified the Q&A pairs from three dimensions: the standardization and accuracy of the questions, the correctness and comprehensiveness of the answers, and whether the text content contains ethical issues or unsafe content.
③ Data with non-standard Q&A were deleted or revised, and entries with safety issues were excluded.
④ Finally, the remaining data were rebalanced in terms of task and quality, followed by a second round of proofreading.

> Q2: Although the supplementary material provides the example of using LLM to score model output, a reference in section 3 and section 4 would make the paper more self-contained.

A2: Thank you for your suggestion. We will add references to the examples of the LLM scoring model outputs in the supplementary materials in Sections 3 and 4 of the paper to make it more self-contained.

> Q3: Due to the source of the benchmark is mainly the Internet and some open-source data corpus, an analysis of data contamination can be important.

A3: Thank you for your suggestion. We recognize the importance of data contamination analysis in benchmark evaluation. The Table 2 in supplementary material categorizes data collection methods into five types. Among them, M1, M3, and M5 indicates that the question-and-answer pairs are constructed by humans or LLMs after distilling knowledge from texts, so these question-and-answer pairs have not been publicly disclosed on the Internet, thereby avoiding data contamination as much as possible. However, the real questions collected from the web (M2) and the reused data from other evaluation datasets (M4) may indeed lead to data contamination. Among them, the proportion of M2-type questions is 7.8%. Although there is a risk of data contamination, its proportion in the entire dataset is relatively low, so the impact of data contamination is relatively small. As for the M4-type questions, since open-source evaluation datasets are prohibited from being used for the training of LLMs, developers should follow relevant data specifications and should not include evaluation datasets in the training corpus to ensure the effectiveness and reliability of the benchmark.

> Q4: A quantitive comparison with other benchmarks would improve the value of this work.

A4: Thank you for your suggestions. A partial comparison of WenMind with other evaluation datasets can be referred to in Table 1 of the main text. The analysis is detailed below: (1) General domain evaluation datasets (C-Eval, CMMLU, etc.) include a small amount of CCLLA domain data, but the analysis of the evaluation results mainly focuses on aspects such as the difficulty of different questions, the comprehensive performance of humanities and social sciences, and does not provide core analytical viewpoints on the CCLLA domain. (2) Other evaluation datasets in the CCLLA field (ACLUE, WYWEB, etc.) mainly assess the model's understanding of classical Chinese. However, these datasets have a limited number of tasks and lack diverse question formats, which restricts a comprehensive assessment of the model's capabilities. In contrast, WenMind has a clear advantage in terms of the number of tasks, diversity of question formats, and comprehensive evaluation, providing experimental analysis from multiple perspectives such as tasks, dimensions, question difficulty, and data fine-tuning, reflecting the model's real capabilities and potential shortcomings in the CCLLA field.

> Q5: The code to evaluate a model with WenMind is not available by the time of the review.

A5: We ensure to provide the related source codes on Github as soon as possible.

Thank you for your detailed and thoughtful review. Here are our responses to your concerns.

---

> Q1: Questions on data quality. Adding a new sub-domain of WenMind will intensify the benchmark.

A1: Thank you for your attention to the quality of the dataset. The difference between classical Chinese and modern Chinese characters lies in the different character shapes; classical Chinese traditionally uses traditional Chinese characters, while our dataset samples use simplified Chinese characters. In response to this issue, we plan to release a new version of the dataset, adding a "Traditional Chinese Literature Understanding" section. The tasks and questions of this section will be constructed using ancient documents written in traditional Chinese characters, such as "Zuo Zhuan" (https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/docs/LDC2017T14/) and "The Twenty-Four Histories" (https://osf.io/cgmjd), to ensure that the model's performance in handling traditional Chinese classical Chinese can be more accurately evaluated. We will explain the additional sections in the final version of the supplementary materials. 

> Q2: Lack of details on data construction.

A2: Thank you for your inquiry. We will provide a more detailed process of data collection and review in the final version of the supplementary materials.

(1) Data Collection Process

Table 2 in the supplementary materials categorizes the data collection methods into five types. Here is a detailed explanation:

① Data collected from the internet. Collectors: Volunteer A, Volunteer B, and Graduate Student C. Collection process: Based on common tasks in Chinese language exams (reading comprehension, understanding-based recitation, etc.), collect high-quality exam questions made by experts and scholars from the internet. We require that the questions should be closely matched with the tasks.

② Other open-source datasets. Collector: Graduate Student D. Collection process: The data collector conducts research and collection of existing open-source datasets, selects classic tasks and high-quality data in the CCLLA field, and assesses the scarcity and construction difficulty of task data. Ultimately, valuable and currently scarce data are selected for reuse to supplement and improve the evaluation benchmark. Post-processing: a. Text filtering: Perform operations such as handling of abnormal symbols (e.g., blank squares), deletion of irrelevant content (e.g., "\r"), and after manual inspection, obtain complete and high-quality data. b. Question writing: Construct Q&A pairs oriented by the needs of different tasks. c. Standardization of format: Questions for the same task are unified into the same questioning method. We directly set up corresponding question templates according to different tasks.

③ LLMs. Collector: Graduate Student E. The construction process refers to lines 123-126 of the main text.

④ Unicode-level data cleaning. Thank you for your reminder. The inconsistency of symbols mainly exists in punctuation marks. In response, we first clarified the language of the questions and answers. For Chinese, we uniformly use Chinese punctuation marks, and for English, we uniformly use English punctuation marks. We have released a new version.


(2) Data Review Process

① Reviewers: The review is conducted by three individuals, namely Volunteer A, Graduate Student D, and Graduate Student E.
② A total of approximately 7000 data entries were collected. The reviewers manually verified the Q&A pairs from three dimensions: the standardization and accuracy of the questions, the correctness and comprehensiveness of the answers, and whether the text content contains ethical issues or unsafe content.
③ Data with non-standard Q&A were deleted or revised, and entries with safety issues were excluded.
④ Finally, the remaining data were rebalanced in terms of task and quality, followed by a second round of proofreading..

> Q3: Questions on Evaluation metrics.

A3: (1) The criteria used for multiple-choice questions are explained in the main text from lines 183 to 186. We adopted a LLM scoring method. The scoring evaluation method we used for multiple-choice questions has significant advantages over traditional metrics like Exact Match (EM) or Hamming distance, which can lead to substantial errors when evaluating different response patterns from various LLMs. Our scoring mechanism can more accurately capture the actual performance of the model, effectively avoiding the errors that traditional evaluation methods may cause. 

(2) In addition to the F1 score and BLEU, we will include traditional metrics such as ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, and Perplexity to enhance the evaluation results. We greatly appreciate your suggestion. Due to space limitations, only ROUGE-L metrics of some models are listed here. We will provide the complete data of traditional metrics in the final version of the supplementary material.

|Model| BLEU |ROUGE-L|
|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|
|ERNIE-4.0-8K-0329|62.8|55.6|
|Yi-1.5-34B-Chat|61.4|50.6|
|Qwen1.5-14B-Chat|62.3|52.0|

A4: Thank you for pointing out the shortcomings in the format of our paper. We will revise the title of the second section to "Related Work" according to your suggestions and re-render the quotation marks in the tables.

A5: Thank you for your suggestions on the paper. We recognize the importance of discussing other ancient language benchmarks, such as Ancient Greek, Han-Korean Classical Chinese, and Ancient Egyptian. In the final version of the paper, we will include a discussion on this aspect.

Thank you for your positive feedback and insightful review. 

---

> Q1: The main area for improvement that I see are in providing some analysis of what makes Chinese Classical Literature and Language challenging for LLMs.

A1: The significant differences between classical Chinese and modern Chinese in terms of grammar, lexicon and expression make the evaluation of LLMs in this field particularly challenging. Classical Chinese texts are usually concise and refined, with free word order, often employing rhetorical devices such as ellipsis and metonymy, and containing a wealth of historical and cultural allusions and specific ancient vocabulary. Compared to modern Chinese, classical Chinese exhibit stronger polysemy and metaphor, which requires LLMs to have a higher level of comprehension and generation capabilities. Currently, the vocabulary of LLMs consists of modern Chinese words, which significantly differs from the vocabulary of classical Chinese, also posing a challenge for current LLMs. Moreover, the unique value of classical Chinese in linguistics is reflected in their inheritance and expression of Chinese traditional culture and philosophical thoughts. Studying ancient texts not only helps to understand Chinese history and culture but also enriches the research methods of linguistics.
From the experimental results, the LLaMA model, after fine-tuning with modern Chinese instruction data to obtain the LLaMA-Chinese series of models, only achieved the highest score of 37.3, reflecting the significant differences between classical and modern Chinese that pose a challengeLLMs. Fine-tuning with modern Chinese has adapted the model to modern grammar and vocabulary, while the free word order, complex rhetoric, and historical and cultural background of classical Chinese make it difficult for LLMs to accurately understand and generate, resulting in a lower score. This indicates that existing models need more specialized training to cope with the unique challenges of classical Chinese.

> Q2: The paper would also benefit from some discussion of what, if any, are the limitations of the evaluation data.

A2: Thank you for your suggestions. A portion of our evaluation task is designed to closely align with the practical application needs of LLMs in the field of classical Chinese. For instance, in the education industry, LLMs can assist students in understanding the syntactic structure of classical Chinese (T1), facilitate the conversion between classical and modern Chinese (T2, T3), and engage in the creation and translation of ancient poetry (T14, T16, T18). Concurrently, tasks such as T4 for named entity recognition and T13 for appreciation of ancient poetry hold significant value for academic research and cultural dissemination. These evaluation tasks not only reflect the performance of models in practical applications but also cover a wide range of scenarios. However, we also recognize that some tasks may be more suitable for general assessment and may not fully reflect the complex needs in specific applications, such as T5 punctuation and T6 topic classification. Therefore, in future work, we will further optimize the design of the dataset to better meet the requirements of specific application scenarios.

The reviewers manually verified the Q&A pairs from three dimensions: the standardization and accuracy of the questions, the correctness and comprehensiveness of the answers, and whether the text content contains ethical issues or unsafe content. 
③ Data with non-standard Q&A were deleted or revised, and entries with safety issues were excluded. 
④ Finally, the remaining data were rebalanced in terms of task and quality, followed by a second round of proofreading.

> Q2: Lacks error analysis for where the LLMs make mistakes - are there general patterns that emerge?

A2: Thank you for your feedback. We agree that error analysis is crucial for understanding LLM performance. Due to space constraints, here we illustrate with examples of sentence structure (T1). In the sentence structure task, we found that LLMs' understanding and mastery of elliptical sentences are the weakest, with an average score of only 14.2, about 16 points lower than other types of sentences. LLMs struggle to accurately grasp which part of the classical Chinese sentence is missing and also to answer what the missing part refers to. In the final version of the supplementary material, we will include a complete analysis of the errors made by LLMs. 

> Q3: There could be a bias ERNIE preferring its own answers.

A3: We selected two approaches to investigate the scoring bias of ERNIE.

(1): GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 was used as an alternative scoring model for the five evaluated models. As shown in the table below, the ranking of models remained the same as when scored by ERNIE-4.0-8K-0329, with ERNIE-4.0-8K-0329 still ranking first. This suggests that its leading position is genuine and less affected by scoring bias.

||ERNIE-4.0-8K-0329 as scoring model|GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 score as scoring model|
|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|
|ERNIE-4.0-8K-0329|64.3|79.7|
|Spark-3.5|60.9|77.4|
|Qwen1.5-14B-Chat|54.9|73.7|
|Baichaun2-13B-chat|45.5|66.4|
|Xunzi-Qwen1.5-7b|37.0|59.8|

(2): Manual analysis. We found that: 
1. For objective questions with standard answers, ERNIE essentially judges and scores each one strictly according to the scoring points of the answer, showing a weaker bias. 
2. For subjective questions, we selected Qu writing tasks for analysis. In the Qu writing task, ERNIE-4.0 scored 67, ranking 11th among all models. This indirectly indicates that in subjective tasks, ERNIE-4.0 does not necessarily give high scores to its own answers.

In summary, the scoring bias of models requires a more detailed and comprehensive research process. We will include the relevant discussions in the final version of the supplementary materials. Thank you for your valuable suggestions.


> Q4: What is the performance on automatically generated data using LLMs vs data scraped from the web?

A4: As shown in Table 2 of the supplementary materials, data generated by LLMs is used for creative tasks (T12, T14-1, T14-2, T14-3), while data scraped from the web is used for other tasks (T7, T9, T19, etc.). The two different data construction methods correspond to distinct tasks, making it difficult to compare their performance.

> Q5: Please provide links and descriptions for all sources used to create the dataset.

A5: Table 2 in the supplementary materials provides the data sources and links for different tasks. There are two situations for tasks without links: (1) The data is generated by LLMs. (2) The original data comes from widely available knowledge texts on the Internet (such as high school Chinese knowledge, etc.), and is not limited to specific web pages, making it difficult to provide specific links. We will add relevant descriptions in the final version of the supplementary materials.

title.value: Contributes extensive CCLLA dataset and benchmarks on various LLMs, lacks details about human validation process

summary_and_contributions.value:
The work has the following contributions:
- Introduces a new evaluation benchmark, WenMind, for CCLLA in LLMs covering Ancient Prose, Ancient Poetry, and Ancient Literary Culture.
- Evaluates the performance of 31 LLMs on various tasks in the WenMind benchmark, across both model scoring and traditional metrics
- Analyzes the results of LLM performance on WenMind, providing insights into where LLMs do and do not perform well in the CCLLA domain.

review.value:
The paper is clear and tackles the relevant problem of LLM performance in the CCLLA domain. Some pros are that the dataset is extensive in size, comprising 42 fine-grained tasks, covering various sub-domains, and including multiple types of questions. The evaluation is also extremely thorough with 31 representative LLMs. 

The cons I find are that there is not enough detail on how the human verification of the dataset is performed, since that is key to ensuring factual correctness and safety of content. Additionally, the paper does not contain much error analysis on where the LLMs make mistakes (more details in areas of improvement section).

strengths.value:
- WenMind contributes to the CCLLA domain by improving upon previous datasets by including:
  - More number of tasks 
  - Three categories (ancient prose, poetry, literary culture)
  - Various question formats like MCQs, fill in the blanks, etc.

- Conducts an extensive and thorough evaluation of 31 LLMs (including general Chinese and English models and specialized models) on the WenMind tasks, evaluating across different metrics like model scoring and traditional metrics. 

- Showcases the limitations of existing LLMs performance on the new proposed dataset, highlighting its applicability for improving the performance on CCLLA tasks

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
* More details about how the human verification is done during the dataset collection phase.
  * Eg. Who reviews the LLM generated responses? How do they check for validity, factual accuracy, etc? 
  * Who writes the Q&A for the information gathered from the internet? What instructions did the question generators follow to perform this task?

* Were there any checks done to detect and mitigate offensive or inappropriate content? I encourage you to include analysis on this front. Due to the automatic nature of the dataset creation, there could be unsafe content present. 

* Lacks error analysis for where the LLMs make mistakes - are there general patterns that emerge? Eg. the models not having knowledge of some CCLLA facts / not being able to perform reasoning, making grammatical errors, etc. 

* Since the dataset is created and evaluated by the ERNIE model family, whilst we are also measuring the performance of ERNIE models, there could be a bias for it preferring its own answers. Ideally, a different model can be used for evaluation than the ones we are testing or at least this should be noted as a limitation. Additionally, what is the performance on automatically generated data using LLMs vs data scraped from the web?

limitations.value: For the most part, limitations are covered. The authors can discuss more about how the automated data curation can lead to some errors in the dataset.

correctness.value: Yes, the dataset is constructed soundly - just needs to include more details on the human validation. The paper also includes thorough experiments against various baselines.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Yes, the paper grounds their motivation well in prior CCLLA works and also in the various LLMs to benchmark.

ethics.value: Since a lot of the of the data collection is done automatically from the web or generated through LLMs, there could be noise or harmful data. It is not clear how the human verification is done eg. who reviews and what all they check for correctness and safety. There should be some analysis done to ensure there is no unsafe content in the dataset.

title.value: Review of WenMind: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Chinese Classical Literature and Language Arts

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper provides a benchmark for evaluating LLMs understanding and generation capabilities in Chinese Classical Literature and Language in three subdomains including Ancient Prose, Ancient Poetry, and Ancient Literary Culture. The authors provide details about the sources of evaluation data, limitations of the current state of evaluation, and experimental results across evaluations of multiple models.

review.value:
My review will focus on data and analysis.

This is a strong and interesting paper. The authors clearly identify the gap that their evaluation benchmark seeks to fill and provide substantiation that their methodology covers the capabilities the benchmark is meant to assess. The results of their experiments suggest that there is indeed a need for meaningful evaluation and that models have a long way to go in the domain of Chinese Classical Literature and Language across all subdomains. 

The main area for improvement that I see are in providing some analysis of what makes Chinese Classical Literature and Language challenging for LLMs: how is the language distinct linguistically and how are these distinctions reflected in the experimental results? The paper would also benefit from additional discussion of what, if any, are the limitations of the evaluation.

strengths.value: The contribution of the paper is meaningful and clear. The source of the evaluation data is compelling and the experimental results suggest that this is a major area of improvement for LLMs.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
As mentioned in the review, the paper would be strengthened by additional details about the linguistic differences between Ancient Chinese and Modern Chinese. This would help readers who are not familiar either with Chinese or Ancient Languages in general understand the challenge.

The paper would also benefit from some discussion of what, if any, are the limitations of the evaluation data. It seems evident that there are many useful applications of LLMs that can analyze and generate Ancient Chinese, but it's not clear if the evaluation data has been designed in a way that is directed towards those applications.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper proposes WenMind, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in Classical Chinese Literature and Language Arts (CCLLA). WenMind comprises 4.8K question-answer pairs across 42 tasks and 3 sub-domains. They evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs using WenMind and provide some insights regarding training LLMs for ancient, low-resource languages.

review.value:
While this paper deals with critical research questions that state-of-the-art LLMs struggle with, it lacks details on data construction, evaluation, and analysis. Human evaluation with Classical Chinese experts will verify the WenMind dataset, especially the machine-generated samples.

### Questions on data quality: Classical Chinese written in Simplified Chinese
Even though this paper deals with Classical Chinese, most of the samples in WenMind are written in Simplified Chinese. See the example below of the translation task. The “answer” (彼应诣此。) is a modern language written in Simplified Chinese.
```
 {
   "id": 603,
   "domain": "ancient prose",
   "capability": "understanding",
   "question_format": "QA",
   "coarse_grained_task_zh": "白文翻译",
   "coarse_grained_task_en": "modern Chinese to classical Chinese",
   "fine_grained_task_zh": "白文翻译",
   "fine_grained_task_en": "modern Chinese to classical Chinese",
   "question": "把白话文翻译为文言文：\n他人应来拜访您。",
   "answer": "彼应诣此。"
 }
```
The letter (script) of Classical Chinese is totally different from Simplified Chinese characters which were invented in the 1950s. This is because the web-crawled datasets (Daizhige and all other datasets using Daizhige) have manually transformed Classical Chinese scripts into Simplified Chinese ones, and all following datasets using Daizhige have negligently adopted their texts.

### Lack of details on data construction
This paper lacks details on the data construction process. Specifically, the authors should describe how the series of operations, including text filtering, question, crafting, and format standardization, is conducted (Lines 119–120).
Furthermore, they should provide more details on data post-processing in terms of Unicode-level data cleaning.  It is common in ancient documents that multiple Unicode characters indicating the same letter (especially in punctuation marks) are mixed.

### Questions on Evaluation metrics
The evaluation metric for multiple-choice questions in this paper (Lines 185–186) is not a commonly adopted metric. For multiple-choice questions, it’s more common to adopt an exact-match (EM) score and/or hamming score measuring the overlap between ground truth and predicted labels. The authors should elaborate more on their evaluation metric choices.
Additionally, incorporating more traditional metrics other than the F1-score and BLEU (e.g., Rouge-L for translation) will intensify the evaluation results.

### Presentation details
Please change the title of section 2 to Related Work (Line 58). See https://english.stackexchange.com/questions/55898/related-work-or-related-works for the details. 
The quotation marks in the caption of Table 1 should be re-rendered. See https://tex.stackexchange.com/questions/531/what-is-the-best-way-to-use-quotation-mark-glyphs for the details.

strengths.value: See the summary and contributions section.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: Adding a new sub-domain of WenMind will intensify the benchmark. The authors can construct question-answer pairs for understanding capabilities (e.g., word/sentence-level understanding, translation) using veritable records of China written in Classical Chinese (e.g., Ming Veritable Records (Ming Shilu), History of Ming (Mingshi), Qing Veritable Records (Qing Shilu), etc).

limitations.value: Yes, the paper adequately addressed their limitations and potential impact in section 6.

correctness.value: While the WenMind benchmark is meticulously constructed, several questions remain in the data construction and evaluation process. See reviews for the details.

clarity.value: Yes, the paper was easy to read and well-written.

relation_to_prior_work.value: They sufficiently discussed previous work of language modeling in the Classical Chinese domain. Still, discussion on other ancient language benchmarks (e.g., ancient Greek, Hanja–Korean Classical Chinese–, ancient Egyptian, etc) in terms of what tasks and challenges have been dealt with in ancient language modeling.

documentation.value: The paper provides a URL to access the dataset, but they also should provide detailed README when the data is publicly available, which is mostly stated in supplementary materials.

ethics.value: There is no ethical issue regarding this paper.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper presents a benchmark for evaluating Chinese classical literature and language arts. It extends the type of tasks to make a more extensive evaluation. The authors collects data for evaluation from multiple resources, then designs a deliberate process pipeline to generate the benchmark dataset. The paper also performs evaluations on multiple categories of models to show the value of the benchmark.

strengths.value:
- The tasks for WenMind are deliberately designed and fine-trained, covering an extensive range of aspects for the Chinese literature and language arts understanding.
- The authors perform a sweep of experiments and analysis on the result using their benchmark to examine multiple types of models.
- The paper is well written and easy to follow. The authors smoothly organize the storyline to introduce data construction and the evaluation.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- The paper lacks explanation of some technical details to create the benchmark dataset. For example, in the Data Collection paragraph of section 3.2, the authors mentioned that they crawled data from open-source corpus and performed question crafting. However, the method to create questions based on existing knowledge data is not provided. Besides, although the supplementary material provides the example of using LLM to score model output, a reference in section 3 and section 4 would make the paper more self-contained.
- Due to the source of the benchmark is mainly the Internet and some open-source data corpus, an analysis of data contamination can be important.
- A quantitive comparison with other benchmarks would improve the value of this work. For example, some analysis showing that WenMind provides a more comprehensive evaluation than existing works can be helpful.

limitations.value: The code to evaluate a model with WenMind is not available by the time of the review.

title.value: WenMind: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Chinese Classical Literature and Language Arts

value: Classical Chinese Literature and Language Arts

TLDR.value: We constructed a comprehensive benchamrk for evaluating large language models in classical Chinese literature and language arts.

abstract.value:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant advancements across numerous domains, but their capabilities in Chinese Classical Literature and Language Arts (CCLLA) remain largely unexplored due to the limited scope and tasks of existing benchmarks. To fill this gap, we propose WenMind, a comprehensive benchmark dedicated for evaluating LLMs in CCLLA. WenMind covers the sub-domains of Ancient Prose, Ancient Poetry, and Ancient Literary Culture, comprising 4,875 question-answer pairs, spanning 42 fine-grained tasks, 3 question formats, and 2 evaluation scenarios: domain-oriented and capability-oriented. Based on WenMind, we conduct a thorough evaluation of 31 representative LLMs, including general-purpose models and ancient Chinese LLMs. The results reveal that even the best-performing model, ERNIE-4.0, only achieves a total score of 64.3, indicating significant room for improvement of LLMs in the CCLLA domain. We also provide insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different LLMs and highlight the importance of pre-training data in achieving better results.
Overall, WenMind serves as a standardized and comprehensive baseline, providing valuable insights for future CCLLA research. 
Our benchmark and related code are available at \url{https://github.com/SCUT-DLVCLab/WenMind}.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
